Question: At the beginning of the school year, \(50\%\) of all students in Mr. Wells’ math class answered “Yes” to the question “Do you love math”, and \(50\%\) answered “No.” At the end of the school year, \(70\%\) answered “Yes” and \(30\%\) answered “No.” Altogether, \(x\%\) of the students gave a different answer at the beginning and end of the school year. What is the difference between the maximum and the minimum possible values of \(x?\)
Solution:
A student who changes answers switches either from No to Yes or from Yes to No. These two groups are disjoint and together contain everyone counted by \(x\).

The Yes share rises from \(50\%\) to \(70\%\), an increase of 20 percentage points. At least \(20\%\) of the class must therefore change answers. This minimum is attainable: let \(20\%\) of the class switch from No to Yes and let everyone else keep the same answer. The final shares are then \(70\%\) Yes and \(30\%\) No, with \(x=20\).

For the maximum, at most \(50\%\) of the class can switch from No to Yes, because only \(50\%\) initially answered No. At most \(30\%\) can switch from Yes to No, because only \(30\%\) finally answered No. Consequently,
\[
x\le 50+30=80.
\]
This bound is also attainable: let all of the initial \(50\%\) who answered No switch to Yes. Of the initial Yes group, let \(30\%\) of the whole class switch to No and the remaining \(20\%\) stay with Yes. The final Yes share is \(50\%+20\%=70\%\), and the changed share is \(80\%\).

Thus the required difference between the maximum and minimum values of \(x\) is
\[
80-20=\boxed{60},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
